details:
We developed The South Side of the Moon, a web app for evaluating landing sites at the lunar south pole. Users choose a site from a catalog of Apollo and CLPS landings and planned Artemis regions, or click any point on the terrain map. For the chosen site and date, the app shows Sun elevation, Earth visibility and the direct-to-Earth link window, plus a timeline that plays these conditions through the lunar day. Each site gets a verdict first ("viable" or not, and which criterion failed), then the details: a 360° panorama of the real horizon with the Sun and Earth on it, a sky plot, a 3D view of the terrain, the next 30 days of sunlight and Earth contact, solar power per square metre, and which Deep Space Network antennas can reach it. Up to four sites can be compared side by side.

How it works: a Python pipeline reads LRO LOLA elevation models of the south pole and computes the true horizon around each point. NAIF SPICE ephemerides then give the exact direction of the Sun, the Earth and the DSN stations at any time. A horizon atlas covers everything from 83°S to the pole at 240 m resolution, so any point on the map can be analysed, not just catalog sites. Results are stored in PostGIS and served by a web API to the browser.

The challenge asks for a tool that turns ephemeris and topographic data into fast, intuitive comparisons. The South Side of the Moon brings NAIF SPICE ephemerides and LRO LOLA terrain together in one interface, replacing the several specialist tools planners would otherwise use. The Landing Windows view shows, for each saved site, the dates when it meets the mission profile and how many days a landing can slip before it stops being viable.

Benefits and impact: at the south pole, where water ice draws future missions, the Sun barely clears the horizon. Small changes in location or date can decide whether a mission has power and contact with Earth. The South Side of the Moon helps teams react quickly to schedule changes, and its guided tour makes these constraints clear to students and the public. To make the results something people can trust, we checked them against JPL Horizons, NASA's LOLA illumination maps and real landings, and published the comparison inside the app. Any view can be shared as a link or exported as a Mission Brief PDF, CSV or JSON, and a documented public API is available.

Tools: Python 3.12 (NumPy, Numba, SpiceyPy, rasterio, pyproj, Zarr) for the science pipeline; FastAPI, PostgreSQL/PostGIS and Redis for the backend; TiTiler for map tiles; WeasyPrint for the PDF reports; TypeScript, React, Vite, OpenLayers and Three.js for the web app; Vitest and Playwright for testing; Docker for deployment. An optional assistant built on Anthropic's Claude answers questions using the app's own data. No special hardware was needed: everything runs on an ordinary desktop PC, which also hosts the live site. The data comes from NASA: LRO LOLA elevation models and illumination maps, and NAIF SPICE kernels, including the DSN station kernels.

Creativity: we treated the problem like a weather forecast for the Moon. You get the answer first, and the evidence after that. The sky view draws the Sun and Earth at their true apparent size against the real horizon, so you can see when the Sun only half clears a ridge. The guided tour runs the app itself to explain the grazing Sun, the wobbling Earth and permanent shadow.

Factors we considered: speed against accuracy (heavy calculations are done ahead of time, so answers take seconds); being honest about uncertainty (each site shows a terrain-confidence rating, and a validation page shows where the model agrees with NASA data and where it doesn't); different audiences (mission profiles with editable limits for planners, and plain language plus the tour for everyone else); and accessibility (English and Portuguese, light and dark themes, keyboard shortcuts and a layout that works on phones).
